passages.t: ‘I lift up my eyes to the hills’
passages.happening:
Psalm 121 is the second Song of Ascents. It begins with a traveller looking up. “A song of ascents. I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come?” (verse 1).

He answers his own question at once. “My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth” (verse 2).

That is the whole of the first part: one question and one answer. But the rest of the psalm grows out of it.
passages.hearers:
Picture a pilgrim on the road to Jerusalem, as the note on Psalm 120 describes. Travel was on foot, on stony paths through the hills. The road was hard, the sun was hot, and the hills could hide robbers. Jesus' story of the man who was beaten and left by the road to Jericho assumes that such roads were dangerous (Luke 10:30).

The hills in verse 1 can be read two ways, and both are held. They may be the hills around Jerusalem, the goal of the trip, which the pilgrim sees with longing. Then the question means: I am almost there; where does my help come from? From the God who lives on that hill. Or they may be the threatening heights along the way, where shrines to other gods often stood. Then the question means: will my help come from the gods of the high places? No.

Either way, the answer looks past the hills to the one who made them. The LORD is ‘the Maker of heaven and earth’. The hills are his work. Help does not come from the hills, but from the One who made them.

This phrase, ‘Maker of heaven and earth’, appears more than once in these songs. Psalm 124 ends with it, and Psalm 134 uses it in its last blessing.
passages.later:
Jesus also looked up and prayed when he faced the tomb of his friend Lazarus: “Jesus lifted His eyes upward and said, ‘Father, I thank You that You have heard Me’” (John 11:41).

Hebrews calls believers to look in one direction: “Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith” (Hebrews 12:2).
passages.asks:
Where do you look first when you need help? To money, to people, to your own strength? None of those is evil. But Psalm 121 asks you to look past them, the way the pilgrim looked past the hills, to the One who made them all.

Verse 1 is a good question to ask out loud on a hard morning. Verse 2 is a good answer to learn by heart.

passages.t: ‘The LORD is your keeper’: guarded going out and coming in
passages.happening:
Now another voice speaks to the traveller, and calls him ‘you’. “He will not allow your foot to slip; your Protector will not slumber” (verse 3). “Behold, the Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (verse 4).

“The LORD is your keeper; the LORD is the shade on your right hand” (verse 5). “The sun will not strike you by day, nor the moon by night” (verse 6). “The LORD will guard you from all evil; He will preserve your soul” (verse 7). And at the end: “The LORD will watch over your coming and going, both now and forevermore” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
One Hebrew word runs through these verses six times: shamar, to keep, guard or watch. The BSB uses several English words for it: ‘Protector’ (verses 3, 4 and 5), ‘guard’ and ‘preserve’ (verse 7), and ‘watch over’ (verse 8). A first hearer would hear the same word again and again, like a drumbeat: he keeps, he keeps, he keeps.

The voice may be a priest blessing pilgrims as they set out, or a friend, or the traveller speaking to his own heart. The psalm does not say.

The pictures come from the road. A slipping foot on a rocky path could mean a broken leg far from help. A watchman who fell asleep could let enemies in. The LORD never nods off. Shade at the right hand was relief from the sun, which can kill in a dry land. The moon by night stands for the dangers of the dark. ‘Coming and going’ means all of life: setting out and coming home, work and rest, from now on.
passages.later:
Jesus prayed for his disciples, “I am not asking that You take them out of the world, but that You keep them from the evil one” (John 17:15). He told them that not one sparrow falls “apart from the will of your Father” and “So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows” (Matthew 10:29-31).

Paul's list of what cannot separate believers from God's love includes trouble, danger and death itself (Romans 8:35-39). Nothing in it is promised to stay away. Nothing in it can cut them off.
passages.hard:
Verse 7 does not promise that no harm will ever come. The pilgrims who sang this psalm still fell ill, were robbed and died, and the Psalms are full of the prayers of faithful people who suffered. The note on Psalm 91 faces the same question at more length: such psalms promise that God keeps the person who trusts him, not that nothing bad will ever happen to them. Some read ‘all evil’ as the final ruin that God will not allow. ‘Your soul’ in verse 7 means the whole living self, and Christians believe God's keeping of it reaches past death.

If harm has come to you or someone you love, it is not because you trusted God too little.
passages.asks:
Psalm 121 is a blessing to carry out the door. You may pray it over someone you love as they set out, or over yourself when you face a long road.

Which of these words do you need today? A God who keeps your foot from slipping. A keeper who never sleeps when you cannot. Shade when life is too hot. A watch over your going out and your coming in. Ask him for it.
